Burden of Proof for Property Alienation in Inheritance An heir sought the division of a property inherited by intestate succession, but the defendant brother claimed the asset had been sold by the deceased to his wife. The legal classification concerns the dissolution of the inheritance community (Art. 713 c.c.) and the onus probandi regarding the composition of the estate. The interpretative challenge is whether a prior sale can be established through mere allegation or reference to previous failed litigation. The Court ruled that real estate transfers require written proof; without the production of a valid contract, the asset remains part of the inheritance mass.
 Indivisibility and Compulsory Sale under Art. 720 c.c. The estate's sole asset was a small building of approximately 40 sqm with structural issues, including a cellar annexed to an adjacent property. The legal issue involves the assessment of "comoda divisibilità" (convenient divisibility). The problem arises when physical partitioning is unfeasible and no co-heir requests the full attribution of the asset. The Court applied the principle that for indivisible assets, in the absence of an assignment request, the judge must order a judicial sale to distribute the monetary proceeds among the heirs.
 Tacit Acceptance through Procedural Participation One co-heir had previously initiated legal action for the division of the same estate in a separate proceeding. This involves the legal principle of "accettazione tacita" (tacit acceptance) under Art. 476 c.c.. The interpretative challenge was whether such procedural conduct confirms the status of heir. The Court clarified that requesting the division of the inheritance mass constitutes an act that necessarily implies the quality of heir, making further formal acceptance or deadlines under Art. 481 c.c. unnecessary.
